titre: Paris, 1563: Merchants Elected to Judge Merchants
accroche: By an edict of 1563, Charles IX creates a court of merchants in Paris. One judge, four consuls: the ancestor of commercial courts.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1563, King Charles IX signs an edict, inspired by his chancellor Michel de L'Hospital, establishing in Paris a consular jurisdiction: a court whose judges are merchants. It is not the first of its kind in France: according to Wikipedia, the first consular jurisdiction is born in Lyon in 1419, followed by those of Toulouse in 1549 and Rouen in 1556 (according to Universalis, the consuls of Toulouse bore the title of *capitouls*). But the 1563 edict establishes the one in the capital and allows others to be created wherever a city requests it.

The formula is simple. The court consists of a judge and four consuls, all merchants. Merchants elect them: in Paris, it is the six merchant guilds, along with the wine merchants and the booksellers, that designate the officeholders. The court hears disputes between merchants, without the formalities of ordinary trials. It deals with bankruptcies and simple insolvencies only from 1715. These merchant judges are called consuls or judges-consuls, hence the name consular jurisdiction.

The contrast with ordinary judges is sharp: the consuls are merchants, elected by the leading merchants. The justice they dispense is described by the Universalis encyclopedia as simple, inexpensive, based on the criterion of good faith, with a very reduced procedure.

## A Model That Gets Copied

The system spreads. In the 18th century, sixty-seven cities have a court of this type, which hears cases at first instance, with appeal to the parlement, and with final authority up to 500 livres. The parlements, from which it removes many cases, oppose it. The institution, born in Lyon in 1419 according to Wikipedia and established in Paris in 1563, offers merchants a simple and inexpensive justice, rendered by merchants.

## What the Model Reveals

The idea is to entrust a quarrel among merchants to a peer rather than to an ordinary judge. Universalis describes the consular jurisdiction as the “ancestor of our commercial court,” and the law of August 16 and 24, 1790 gives these courts the name of commercial courts (*tribunaux de commerce*).

But the same idea raises a question that 1563 does not settle: the person who knows the trade is also the person who has its interests. A court of peers gains in competence what it risks losing in distance.

repere.texte: In the 18th century, sixty-seven French cities have a consular jurisdiction, which hears cases at first instance with appeal to the parlement, and without appeal up to 500 livres.

carte.punch: In 1563, Paris gets judges who are also merchants.
carte.idee: The edict of 1563 establishes in Paris a court of merchants elected by their peers: one judge and four consuls, without the formalities of ordinary trials. In the 18th century, sixty-seven cities have one.

quiz.question: Why did the parlements oppose the consular jurisdictions created from 1563 on?
choix: They applied canon law instead of royal law
They reserved commercial cases to noblemen of the robe alone
They demanded higher fees from litigants than the parlements did
They took many cases away from them, in favor of merchant judges
quiz.explication: According to Universalis, the consuls offered simple, inexpensive justice with a reduced procedure, and the parlements opposed it because it took many cases away from them. It was neither more expensive, nor canonical, nor reserved to nobles.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when did the first consular jurisdiction appear in France, according to Wikipedia?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, the first consular jurisdiction is born in Lyon in 1419; Toulouse (1549) and Rouen (1556) follow, then Paris with the edict of 1563: Paris is therefore not the first.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who elects the judges of the Parisian consular jurisdiction?
choix: The king, on the proposal of his chancellor L'Hospital
The parlements, which wanted to keep control
The merchants themselves, through their guilds
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Merchants elect the judges: in Paris, the six merchant guilds, along with the wine merchants and the booksellers, designate the officeholders.
